tier_reason: First-party Fraunhofer HHI wiki (Encoder-Performance.md, last edited 2026-03-30) gives Table III speedups of VVenC v1.14.0 (8 threads) over VTM-19.2 and HM-17.0 (single-threaded) on AMD EPYC 7502P, but no timing harness is published (repo cfg/ holds only preset configs) and compiler and flags are not stated, so it cannot be A. The peer-reviewed VVenC papers (ICMEW 2021 and later) are on blocked IEEE/ACM/arXiv/ResearchGate pages, so their numbers are snippet only and cannot lift the tier to B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: VVenC v1.14.0 Table III, 8 threads vs single-threaded reference encoders, random access, JVET CTC: HD4K speedup over VTM-19.2 faster 2400x, fast 1100x, medium 330x, slow 87x, slower 19x (HD column 2400x/1100x/280x/74x/15x; UHD column 2500x/1200x/380x/98x/22x); over HM-17.0 the HD4K speedups are 380x/180x/53x/14x/3x with PSNR-YUV BD-rate versus HM of -13.3%/-25.8%/-35.1%/-39.1%/-42.1%. Only the slower preset matches VTM's compression (Figure 1 puts VTM-19.2 at roughly -41% BD-rate versus HM, read approximately from the figure), so the quality-matched speedup over VTM is 15x HD / 22x UHD / 19x HD4K, and it includes 8 threads versus 1. The page prose says 'more than 20x for HD4K' for slower and quotes 2300x/370x/-13.7% (faster) and 280x/45x/-35.8% (medium) for HD4K, which disagree with the v1.14.0 table and look stale. Versus x265 3.5 (8 threads) there are no numbers, only Figure 2: x265's plotted presets sit at about +29% to +42% PSNR BD-rate versus HM at about 0.4% to 6% of HM's runtime, while VVenC's presets sit at -13% to -42% at about 0.26% to 33% of HM's runtime (read approximately from Figure 2, derived from page data), i.e. a compression win at similar runtime rather than a speed win over x265.
corrections.workload: Random-access encoding of JVET common-test-condition sequences (class B HD, classes A1/A2 UHD) at constant QP 22/27/32/37; VVenC v1.14.0 with 8 threads versus single-threaded VTM-19.2 and HM-17.0 (both with MCTF enabled), reported as encoder runtime speedup together with PSNR-YUV BD-rate versus HM-17.0. The x265 3.5 runs in Figure 2 use 8 threads, --tune psnr and CRF 17/22/27/32 instead of constant QP.
corrections.caveats: First-party wiki numbers; compiler, flags and thread pinning are not stated and no timing harness is published, so not reproducible-tier. The measured code does different work from the baselines: VVenC runs 8 threads while VTM and HM are single-threaded, and every preset except slower gives up compression relative to VTM (faster loses roughly 28 BD-rate points against VTM), so the 2400x headline compares a fast, lower-quality multi-threaded VVC encode with the single-threaded JVET reference encoder. VTM and HM are research reference encoders, not production encoders; the category baselines x264/x265 are a different codec generation and VVenC is not shown to be faster than them in wall-clock time: the x265 3.5 comparison exists only as figures (CRF rate control versus constant QP for VVenC; the reference [14] links the x265 Release_3.4 tree while the text says v3.5), and third-party search snippets (forasoft.com, dev.to; not opened, blocked) describe vvenc medium as far slower than x265 medium on wall clock. The page prose disagrees with its own Table III (e.g. slower 'more than 20x' versus 19x HD4K in the table). Peer-reviewed first-party papers (ICMEW 2021: snippet only, single-threaded VVenC at 46% of VTM runtime and fastest configuration over 140x faster than VTM for an early version) were not opened. License is the Clear BSD License (BSD-3-Clause-Clear), which is FSF-libre but not OSI-approved per the SPDX license list 3.29.0, and it explicitly grants no patent rights; H.266/VVC itself is covered by patent pools. Page last edited 2026-03-30.

notes: All Table III numbers in the record match the v1.14.0 wiki table; metadata (1.2k stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-10-02) confirmed. Usability changed to reference only because SPDX marks BSD-3-Clause-Clear as not OSI-approved (it is BSD-3-Clause plus an explicit no-patent-grant clause); the orchestrator may prefer to treat it as copyable by policy. The record is a fair VTM/HM comparison but not evidence of beating x264/x265 on speed; consider a shortcoming saying the speed win is versus the VVC reference encoder only.
